result: The authors identified 190 high-confidence eRNAs in mouse liver using RNA-seq and genomic analysis, with 14 upregulated and 5 downregulated by GW4064 treatment. Fincor was identified as one of the most robustly induced eRNAs (>10-fold induction), with transient expression peaking at 1 hour. Adjacent genes to Fincor did not change expression after acute FXR activation.
evaluation: All three reviewers praised the 'unbiased transcriptional profiling' and 'state-of-the-art methodology' used to identify eRNAs. One reviewer specifically noted 'The use of GRO-seq and RNA-seq technologies has provided an in-depth and unbiased view of the transcriptional alterations driven by the FXR agonist.' No concerns were raised about the identification or characterization of Fincor as a robustly induced eRNA.

result: The authors demonstrated that FXR-induced eRNAs, including Fincor, were activated transcriptionally by GW4064 in Fxr-flox mice but not in Fxr-LKO mice. FXR and RXRα recruitment to the Fincor enhancer region increased substantially after GW4064 treatment, along with BRD4 occupancy. An IR1 motif (FXR binding site) was identified and validated by luciferase reporter assays, demonstrating that GW4064-activated FXR directly upregulates Fincor expression.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly praised the 'biochemical characterization of FincoR using FXR-KO mice combined with Gro-seq and Luciferase reporter assays' which 'convincingly demonstrates this eRNA as a FXR transcriptional target sensitive to FXR agonists.' The editor noted the study 'reports a fundamental discovery' with 'convincing findings.' No concerns were raised about the mechanistic demonstration of FXR-mediated Fincor induction.

result: The authors characterized Fincor as a liver-enriched, nuclear, polyadenylated eRNA that is highly expressed in liver with minimal expression in other tissues. RACE identified one transcript of ~3.7 kb, though RNA-seq suggested additional isoforms >10 kb. PhyloCSF analysis and in vitro translation assays confirmed Fincor lacks protein-coding potential. GW4064 treatment increased nuclear abundance of Fincor.
evaluation: Reviewers commended the 'biochemical characterization' and noted the study provides 'validation in mouse models.' One reviewer stated 'The subsequent biochemical characterization of FincoR...convincingly demonstrates this eRNA as a FXR transcriptional target.' The characterization of Fincor as a liver-specific lncRNA was not questioned by any reviewer.

result: The authors demonstrated that Fincor is specifically induced by hammerhead-type FXR agonists (GW4064, cilofexor, tropifexor) but not by other FXR agonists (OCA, fexaramine) or the natural bile acid cholic acid. This specificity was observed at 1 hour treatment, and even extended OCA treatment (4 hours or 1 week) failed to induce Fincor.
evaluation: Reviewers highlighted this as a key finding, with one noting 'Incorporation of tropifexor, an investigational FXR agonist in clinical trials, alongside these experimental models bridges experimental findings to potential therapeutic applications.' The agonist-specific induction pattern was not challenged and was viewed as strengthening the study's translational relevance.

result: Using CRISPR/Cas9-mediated liver-specific knockdown, the authors achieved ~60% downregulation of Fincor specifically in liver. Under physiological conditions, this did not significantly alter liver metabolites (triglyceride, cholesterol, BA, glycogen) or serum NEFA. RNA-seq revealed 18 upregulated and 53 downregulated genes, with downregulated genes enriched in pathways involving fatty acid oxidation, organelle organization, and metabolic processes. Neighboring genes remained unchanged.
evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the knockdown approach or the physiological findings. One reviewer noted 'The study's design, with the inclusion of both negative and positive controls...ensures that the observed therapeutic effects can be confidently attributed to FincoR's modulation.' The lack of metabolic phenotype under normal conditions was not criticized.

result: In NASH diet-fed mice, tropifexor treatment markedly reduced liver triglycerides and neutral lipids (Oil Red O staining), and decreased expression of genes involved in BA synthesis (Cyp7a1, Cyp8b1) and lipid synthesis (Srebp1c, Lpin1, Scd1). These beneficial effects on reducing hepatic steatosis were not altered by Fincor downregulation, indicating tropifexor's anti-steatotic effects are independent of Fincor.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly acknowledged this finding, with one stating the study 'showed that the knockdown of FincoR in a murine NASH model attenuated part of the effect of tropifexor, an FXR agonist, namely inflammation and fibrosis, but not steatosis.' This distinction between steatosis (Fincor-independent) and inflammation/fibrosis (Fincor-dependent) was accepted without challenge.

result: In NASH mice, tropifexor treatment reduced hepatocyte ballooning, apoptosis (TUNEL), fibrosis (Sirius Red), and macrophage infiltration (F4/80), along with decreasing serum ALT/AST and inflammatory markers (IL1β, CCL2). These beneficial effects on inflammation, fibrosis, and apoptosis were markedly diminished by Fincor knockdown. Gene expression analysis confirmed tropifexor reduced pro-fibrotic (Col1a1, Col1a2, Acta2), pro-inflammatory (Eda2r, Ifng, Ccl3), and pro-apoptotic genes (Ctsb, Ctss) while increasing anti-apoptotic genes (Bcl2), with these effects reversed by Fincor downregulation.
evaluation: This is the central finding of the manuscript and was strongly endorsed by all reviewers. One reviewer stated 'They demonstrate that FincoR significantly enhances tropifexor's effectiveness in reducing liver fibrosis and inflammation in NASH, presenting it as a promising therapeutic target.' Another noted the findings have 'therapeutic implications in the treatment of MASH' and are 'convincing.' The use of multiple complementary approaches (histology, serum markers, gene expression) was praised.

result: Hepatic Fincor levels were significantly elevated in multiple mouse models of liver disease, including high-fat diet (HFD), HFD with high fructose, ANIT-induced cholestasis, and bile duct ligation (BDL). These findings suggest Fincor is upregulated in pathological conditions involving dysregulated BA metabolism.
evaluation: Reviewers specifically praised this expansion of the study, noting 'The research expands on the original findings by including diverse mouse models of NAFLD/NASH and cholestatic liver injury...This broadened scope underscores FincoR's involvement in liver disease mechanisms.' The elevation of Fincor in disease models was viewed as strengthening the translational relevance.

result: The authors identified moderate sequence conservation between mouse Fincor and a human genomic region containing an uncharacterized lncRNA (XR_007061585.1). This human lncRNA was elevated in liver samples from PBC and NAFLD patients compared to normal individuals, but not in severe NASH-fibrosis patients, suggesting a potential conserved therapeutic mechanism.
evaluation: Reviewers strongly endorsed this addition to the manuscript, stating 'The manuscript revision includes promising data on the sequence similarity between mouse FincoR and a human locus, identifying a partially conserved human lncRNA (XR_007061585.1) with elevated levels in NAFLD and PBC patients. This addition enhances the study's relevance to human health.' The human data was viewed as a major strength addressing translational potential.

result: The authors conclude that pharmacological activation of FXR by hammerhead-type agonists induces Fincor, which contributes to amelioration of NASH in mice by reducing inflammation, fibrosis, and apoptosis. They propose Fincor may represent a new drug target for metabolic disorders including NASH, and that complete understanding of Fincor's mechanisms may provide novel insights for therapy development.
evaluation: Reviewers endorsed these conclusions, with one stating the study 'provides a framework how one can investigate the role of noncoding genes in pharmacological intervention targeting a known protein coding genes' and noting it 'may provide useful information for improved and individualized treatment for metabolic disorders.' Another called it a 'fundamental discovery' with 'therapeutic implications.' The speculative nature of Fincor as a drug target was implicitly accepted as appropriate for a discovery study.

result: Using bioinformatic analysis (ATtRACT database), the authors identified potential Fincor-binding proteins including KHDRBS1, RBM38, YBX2, and YBX3, which are involved in RNA processing and metabolism. This represents preliminary mechanistic insight into how Fincor may function.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged that 'certain questions remain unanswered within the scope of this study on FincoR, due to feasibility and technical challenges,' they also noted 'Future work to dissect the detailed mechanisms by which FincoR facilitates action of FXR and its agonists is warranted.' The bioinformatic predictions were not validated experimentally, and reviewers implicitly indicated this mechanistic gap as a limitation, though they accepted it as beyond the current scope.
